guide.title: From forces to fading motion
guide.subtitle: What makes an oscillator cross equilibrium while its motion shrinks?

blocks.text: How does a released mass move while a spring restores it and a damper removes energy? Follow forces → differential equation → roots → real motion → initial data, then apply the chain to a new problem.

Prerequisites: Newton’s law, time derivatives, the product rule and complex numbers. Here \(x^{\prime}\) is velocity and \(x^{\prime\prime}\) acceleration. We develop the differential-equation method when it becomes necessary.

blocks.reason: Choose \(x=0\) at equilibrium. The spring force opposes displacement; the viscous damper force opposes velocity. Both are modeling assumptions, not consequences of Newton’s law.
symbols: Spring and damping forces (N); functions of displacement and velocity.

blocks.reason: Move the two forces to the left. The zero on the right states that no external driving force acts.

rows: Time (s); signed displacement from equilibrium (m), the unknown function.
Velocity (m/s); acceleration (m/s²), derivatives of the same \(x(t)\).

blocks.label: Model boundary and next question
blocks.text: Use one coordinate, a linear spring, a velocity-proportional damper and constant m, b, k. Large deformations, dry friction and forcing require a changed equation. Our equation constrains motion, but does not yet give \(x(t)\).

guide.title: Choose an exponential mode
guide.subtitle: Use the constant-coefficient structure before solving for rates

blocks.text: An exponential retains its shape when differentiated. That makes it a useful trial for a linear equation with constant coefficients; it is a method choice, not a claim that the visible motion is a simple exponential.

blocks.latex: x=C e^{\lambda t},\qquad x^{\prime}=\lambda x,\qquad x^{\prime\prime}=\lambda^2 x
blocks.reason: Differentiation multiplies the trial by \(\lambda\) once for each derivative.
symbols: Possibly complex rate (s<super>−1</super>), to be determined; \(i^2=-1\).

blocks.reason: Substitute the trial and its derivatives. Since C is nonzero and the exponential never vanishes, the coefficient must be zero.

blocks.text: The exponential factor stays nonzero, so its coefficient must vanish. The next page solves that characteristic equation and explains why the roots describe decay and oscillation.

guide.title: Find modes the equation preserves
guide.subtitle: Why an exponential trial turns derivatives into algebra

blocks.text: The trial from page 2 requires \(m\lambda^2+b\lambda+k=0\). Its roots determine which rates satisfy the motion equation. Separate the damping rate from the natural angular frequency.

blocks.reason: Divide by \(m>0\) and introduce two rates to separate damping from spring–mass motion.
symbols: Undamped angular frequency (rad/s), fixed. Radians are dimensionless.

blocks.reason: Complete the square. Under \(0<\gamma<\omega_0\), the right side is negative, so the roots form a complex conjugate pair.
Write the square root of the negative number as ±i times a positive rate.
symbols: Damped angular frequency (rad/s); real and positive only in the underdamped regime.

blocks.label: What the roots tell us
blocks.text: The real part \(-\gamma\) produces decay; the imaginary parts \(\pm\omega_{\mathrm{d}}\) produce oscillation. We still need a real displacement and two constants that fit the initial data.

guide.title: Convert complex modes to real motion
guide.subtitle: The product rule carries both the decay and the oscillation

blocks.text: Euler’s identity connects a complex exponential to cosine and sine. Because the equation is linear with real coefficients, the real and imaginary parts of a complex solution are real solutions. Their linear combination can match two independent initial data.

blocks.reason: Use \(e^{i\theta}=\cos\theta+i\sin\theta\); \(\theta=\omega_{\mathrm{d}}t\) is dimensionless.
Use the two real modes. They are independent when \(\omega_{\mathrm{d}}>0\): their initial displacement–velocity pairs are \((1,-\gamma)\) and \((0,\omega_{\mathrm{d}})\).
symbols: Real coefficients (m), determined by initial conditions rather than by m, b, k alone.

blocks.text: For differentiation only, call the trigonometric bracket \(y(t)\), in metres: \(x(t)=e^{-\gamma t}y(t)\). This helper represents the bracket, not the displacement.

blocks.reason: Differentiate the bracket. The chain rule contributes \(\omega_{\mathrm{d}}\) to both trigonometric derivatives.

blocks.latex: x^{\prime}=-\gamma e^{-\gamma t}y+e^{-\gamma t}y^{\prime}=e^{-\gamma t}(y^{\prime}-\gamma y)
blocks.reason: Apply the product rule to the exponential and the bracket; neither is constant.

blocks.label: Why the decay term matters
blocks.text: Differentiating only the trigonometric bracket misses \(-\gamma A\) in the initial velocity. That omission changes B and gives a solution with the wrong launch condition.
We now have the general underdamped form and its velocity. The next page uses \(x(0)\) and \(x^{\prime}(0)\) to select one motion from this family.

guide.title: Let the initial data choose the solution
guide.subtitle: Work the illustrated case, then distinguish displacement from envelope

blocks.text: The new givens \(x_0\) (m) and \(v_0\) (m/s) are the signed initial displacement and velocity. A and B are the real coefficients carried over from page 4.

blocks.reason: Set \(t=0\) in the displacement and in both product-rule terms: the exponential and cosine become 1, and the sine becomes 0.
Rearrange the initial-velocity equation; division is allowed because \(\omega_{\mathrm{d}}>0\). Units of the numerator are m/s, so B has units m.

blocks.text: Illustrated baseline: \(m=1\) kg, \(b=0.4\) kg/s, \(k=4\) N/m, \(x_0=0.10\) m and \(v_0=0\). This is a new numerical illustration of the general model.

blocks.reason: The bracket is a scalar product of (A, B) with (cos θ, sin θ), a unit vector. Its absolute value cannot exceed \(\sqrt{A^2+B^2}\).
symbols: Constant coefficient of the envelope (m); here \(R\approx0.100503782\) m.

blocks.label: The envelope is not the initial displacement
blocks.text: \(A=x_0=0.10\) m, but \(R\approx0.100504\) m because B is nonzero. Release from rest does not require \(B=0\): the exponential also contributes to \(x^{\prime}(0)\). The next page shows this bound over the complete time response.

guide.title: Read oscillation and decay in one graph
guide.subtitle: Use the initial-data solution to distinguish a motion from its bound
guide.source: Authored source-slides.pdf · physical page 3; tutor derivation

blocks.text: The time-response chart uses the baseline from page 5. Its solid curve is displacement; the two dashed curves are \(\pm R e^{-\gamma t}\). Read time in seconds and displacement in metres. The zero crossings show oscillation; the shrinking bounds show decay.

blocks.caption: Original response and envelope plot; source slide 3. Same baseline as page 5.

blocks.text: The dashed curves are bounds, not a line connecting the turning points: the changing exponential shifts extrema away from cosine maxima. The envelope time \(\tau=\frac{1}{\gamma}\) is 5 s: the envelope falls to \(e^{-1}\) of its initial value in 5 s. The oscillatory factor repeats after \(T_{\mathrm{d}}=\frac{2\pi}{\omega_{\mathrm{d}}}\approx3.15742\) s.

blocks.label: What this figure adds
blocks.text: The solid curve crosses equilibrium while the dashed bounds shrink. R depends on both launch conditions; the envelope bounds \(x(t)\) rather than tracing it. Next we use the force law to account for the decreasing mechanical energy.

guide.title: Connect the force law to energy loss
guide.subtitle: An exact power balance explains the decay without assuming a fixed sinusoidal amplitude
guide.source: Authored source-slides.pdf · physical page 3; tutor derivation

blocks.text: The graph from page 6 shows the motion and its bounds. The force law from page 1 supplies an independent check: damping should remove energy whenever the mass moves.

blocks.reason: Mechanical energy is kinetic plus spring potential energy.
Apply the chain rule with m and k fixed, then factor out the velocity.
The equation of motion gives \(mx^{\prime\prime}+kx=-bx^{\prime}\). Damping removes power at a nonnegative rate; kg/s × (m/s)² has units W.

blocks.label: A useful check
blocks.text: At release from rest, \(\frac{dE}{dt}=0\) at that instant, but energy decreases once the mass moves. The identity above is exact; it does not by itself make E(t) exactly proportional to \(e^{-2\gamma t}\).

guide.title: Original practice: select and predict a new motion
guide.subtitle: Full four-part question; worked part (a) starts below
guide.source: Tutor-authored practice P1 · all conditions and parts

blocks.text: A free mass–spring–damper system has \(m=2.0\) kg, \(b=1.2\) kg/s and \(k=18\) N/m. At \(t=0\), \(x_0=0.080\) m and \(v_0=-0.030\) m/s. The spring and damper remain linear and the coefficients remain constant.

rows: Classify the damping and calculate both characteristic roots. Use page 3.
Find A and B, then write the complete real solution \(x(t)\). Use pages 4–5.
Calculate \(x(1.5\,\mathrm{s})\) to three significant figures. Check it against the envelope bound. Use page 5.

Reset to the same m, k, \(x_0\) and \(v_0\), but double b to 2.4 kg/s. Check the regime and compare \(\gamma\), \(\omega_{\mathrm{d}}\), the envelope time \(\tau\) (the reciprocal of \(\gamma\)) and the normalized envelope at 1.5 s. Recalculate R and explain whether equal \(x_0\) means equal R. Use pages 3, 5–7.

blocks.label: Method choice
blocks.text: Use the underdamped solution only after checking \(\gamma<\omega_0\). This is an initial-value problem with no driving force, so two launch conditions select A and B.

blocks.reason: Part (a): substitute the new parameters into the definitions. Here 0.300 < 3.00, so the system is underdamped.
The negative discriminant produces two complex conjugate roots.
Both roots have a negative real part and a nonzero imaginary part: decaying oscillation.

blocks.text: Continue with worked parts (b)–(d) on pages 9–10. These answers use the practice data above, not the chart baseline.

guide.title: Predict motion and check the launch data
guide.subtitle: Original P1(b)–(c) / Select the coefficients and check the envelope

blocks.reason: Part (b): \(A=0.080\) m from the displacement condition. The velocity relation gives B as above. The initial velocity −0.030 m/s includes the exponential derivative; it is not simply \(\omega_{\mathrm{d}}B\).
Use \(\omega_{\mathrm{d}}=2.984962311\) rad/s from page 8, metres for x and seconds for t. Displayed coefficients are rounded; calculations retain full precision. The launch velocity is −0.030 m/s.

blocks.text: Part (c): at \(t=1.5\) s, the phase is 4.477443467 rad and the exponential factor is 0.637628152. Substitute both into the solution, preserving the negative sine coefficient.

blocks.reason: The mass lies on the negative side of equilibrium. Its absolute displacement, 0.0106282 m, is below the envelope 0.0510264 m.

blocks.text: Part (d) continues on page 10. It resets to the same launch conditions and changes only the damping coefficient.

guide.title: Change damping, then refit the launch data
guide.subtitle: Original P1(d) / Reset to the same mass, stiffness, displacement and velocity

blocks.text: Part (d): change only b. The critical value is \(b_{\mathrm{c}}=2\sqrt{mk}=12\) kg/s, so \(b=2.4\) kg/s remains underdamped. Keeping the same launch conditions requires recalculating B and R.

The decay rate doubles and the envelope time halves, while \(\omega_{\mathrm{d}}\) decreases about 1.53%. The normalized envelope isolates this rate change. Equal \(x_0\) does not make R equal: B depends on both changed \(\gamma\) and \(\omega_{\mathrm{d}}\) through the initial-velocity equation on page 5. R is also slightly larger than \(x_0\) in both cases.

blocks.label: Do not compare displacement using the envelope alone
blocks.text: A faster-decaying envelope does not make \(|x(t)|\) smaller at every instant, because phase and frequency also change. At 1.5 s the changed system has \(x\approx-0.0120908\) m, even though its envelope is smaller.

guide.title: Limits reveal when to change methods
guide.subtitle: Transfer the model; do not extend one regime beyond its condition
guide.source: Authored source-slides.pdf · physical pages 1–3; tutor transfer

blocks.text: Undamped limit: if b tends to zero with m and k fixed, \(\gamma\) tends to zero and \(\omega_{\mathrm{d}}\) tends to \(\omega_0\). The exponential disappears and the initial-condition solution becomes ordinary simple harmonic motion.

blocks.reason: Take the limit of the complete solution, including B. The energy identity then gives \(\frac{dE}{dt}=0\).

blocks.text: Critical boundary: when \(\gamma\) tends to \(\omega_0\) from below, \(\omega_{\mathrm{d}}\) tends to zero. The apparent division by \(\omega_{\mathrm{d}}\) is resolved because \(\frac{\sin(\omega_{\mathrm{d}}t)}{\omega_{\mathrm{d}}}\) tends to \(t\); taking the limit of B alone would miss this cancellation.

blocks.reason: Take the limit of the complete expression. At critical damping the repeated-root solution is no longer a sinusoid. For b greater than \(2\sqrt{mk}\), use two real exponential modes instead.

blocks.label: Original transfer check
blocks.text: Double m while keeping b and k fixed. Must an originally underdamped system become overdamped? Use the definitions before answering.

blocks.reason: Answer: no. The ratio of decay rate to undamped angular frequency becomes smaller, so an underdamped system stays underdamped. This prediction assumes the same b and k remain valid when m changes.

blocks.text: Recognition cues: force balance establishes the model; constant coefficients invite exponential trials; complex conjugate roots invite decaying sine and cosine; initial displacement and velocity fix both coefficients. Check the regime before dividing by \(\omega_{\mathrm{d}}\).

Useful next attempt: solve P1 again from the force law without looking at pages 8–10. Check the force units, the initial velocity and the envelope bound. Receiving this guide does not demonstrate mastery.
